`ArticleService.slugify()` = `slug(title, {lower: true}) + '-' + <6 base-36 chars from Math.random()>`.
Two articles with the same title therefore get different slugs. The slug is set once at create;
`update()` has a `// Todo: update slug also when title gets changed` and does not.

### [LESSONS.md] LESSONS.md > Lessons Learned — RealWorld API (NestJS) > Authentication is not authorization (#6, #44)
**What happened:** any logged-in user could `PUT` or `DELETE` any other user's article. The
route is in `AuthMiddleware`'s list, so people assumed it was "protected" — but the middleware
only proves the caller is *a* user, and `ArticleService.update()/delete()` never compare
`req.user.id` with `article.author.id`. The Swagger `403 Forbidden` annotations on those handlers
describe a check that does not exist.

**Rule:** for every mutating route, name the line that compares the caller with the record's
owner. If you cannot, there is no ownership check, whatever the decorators say.

Handlers read `@Body('article')`, `@Body('user')`, `@Body('comment')` — the client sends
`{ "article": {...} }`, never a flat object. New endpoints follow the same nesting.

| column | type | notes |

| id | int PK | |

### [LESSONS.md] LESSONS.md > Lessons Learned — RealWorld API (NestJS) > A relation that is not eager is `undefined`, not `[]`
**What happened:** `ArticleService.favorite()` loads the user with `findOne(id)` and then calls
`user.favorites.findIndex(...)`. `favorites` is a non-eager `@ManyToMany`, so it is `undefined`

`POST /articles/:slug/favorite`. Same pattern in `findAll()` for `?favorited=` (`author.favorites.map`).

**Rule:** before touching `entity.relation` in a service, find the `relations: [...]` or the
`eager: true` that loads it. If neither exists, the property is `undefined`.

### [LESSONS.md] LESSONS.md > Lessons Learned — RealWorld API (NestJS) > Every handler returns the RO envelope, never a bare entity (#57)
**What happened:** `ArticleController.create()` returned `ArticleEntity` directly while every

from its side the request succeeded.

**Rule:** the envelope (`ArticleRO`, `UserRO`, …) is the contract with every RealWorld client.
A handler whose return type is not a `*RO` interface is a bug even if it "works" in Postman.

**Rule:** when a filter is "articles in this set", the column is `article.id`. Read the
`andWhere` literally; do not trust the variable name.

**Rule:** in a controller, any literal path (`feed`, `popular`, `search`) goes above the `:slug`
handler. Order in the class is match order.

  `decoded.user`, which does not exist in the payload → `undefined`.)
- Same `jwt.verify` throw → 500 problem as the middleware.

### [.claude/knowledge/workspace.md] workspace.md > RealWorld API (NestJS) — workspace overview > Conventions (these are the rules, not suggestions) > The response envelope and the `RO` suffix
`RO` means **Response Object**. Every controller method returns the RealWorld envelope, named
`<Thing>RO` in `*.interface.ts`:

| Endpoint family | Returns | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| single article | `ArticleRO` | `{ article: {...} }` |
| list | `ArticlesRO` | `{ articles: [...], articlesCount: n }` |
| comments | `CommentsRO` | `{ comments: [...] }` |
| user | `UserRO` | `{ user: {..., token} }` |
| profile | `ProfileRO` | `{ profile: {..., following} }` |

The frontends read `response.article.slug`, `response.user.token`, etc. A method that returns a
bare entity instead of the envelope breaks every RealWorld client (see `LESSONS.md`).

  shared/pipes/           ValidationPipe

One module per RealWorld resource. Each module owns its controller, service, entity and DTOs.
Module files also own **which routes require auth** — see `auth.md`.

### [.claude/knowledge/workspace.md] workspace.md > RealWorld API (NestJS) — workspace overview > Conventions (these are the rules, not suggestions) > Layer order
`controller → service → repository/entity`. Controllers do no business logic and never touch a
repository; services do. Cross-module data (e.g. the article service needs users and follows)
is reached by injecting that module's repository via `TypeOrmModule.forFeature([...])` in the
importing module — see `article.module.ts`.

### [.claude/knowledge/auth.md] auth.md > Authentication and authorization > Authorization (ownership) — where it is enforced
**Nowhere.** The middleware answers "is this a valid user"; no service or controller method
compares the caller with the record's owner:

| Action | Ownership check |
|---|---|
| `PUT /articles/:slug` | none — `ArticleService.update(slug, body)` does `Object.assign(article, body)` and saves |
| `DELETE /articles/:slug` | none — `delete({slug})` |
| `DELETE /articles/:slug/comments/:id` | none — and comments have no author to compare against anyway |
| `DELETE /users/:slug` | none, and unguarded |
| `PUT /user` | implicitly the caller (`@User('id')`), fine |

The Swagger `@ApiResponse({ status: 403 })` lines on the article controller describe an
intended behaviour, not an implemented one — nothing returns 403.

text:
**Refined prompt:** Answer whether two articles created with identical titles end up with the same slug in this NestJS RealWorld API, from the perspective of a senior engineer on the codebase, citing the generating code and the DB constraint, in a short answer-first form · Assumptions: "slug" = the article slug produced at create time (not user/profile identifiers), and you care about both the happy path and what happens if a collision does occur.

**No — the slug gets a random suffix, so identical titles produce different slugs.** But nothing *enforces* uniqueness, so a collision is unlikely rather than impossible, and if one happened the database would silently accept it.

**The generator** — `src/article/article.service.ts:201-203`:

```ts
  slugify(title: string) {
    return slug(title, {lower: true}) + '-' + (Math.random() * Math.pow(36, 6) | 0).toString(36)
  }
```

Two "How to train your dragon" articles become `how-to-train-your-dragon-4xk1p9` and `how-to-train-your-dragon-m20zqa`. Called once, at create: `article.slug = this.slugify(articleData.title);` (`src/article/article.service.ts:175`).

**No unique constraint** — `src/article/article.entity.ts:11-12`:

```ts
  @Column()
  slug: string;
```

Plain `@Column()`, no `{unique: true}`, and `synchronize: true` builds the table from this — so the DB will not reject a duplicate. Odds are ~1 in 2.18 billion (36⁶) per pair, but if it ever hit, the second insert succeeds and `findOne({slug})` (`src/article/article.service.ts:102, 115, 132, 148, 166, 191, 198`) returns whichever row comes first — the other article becomes unreachable, and a `PUT`/`DELETE` on that slug would edit the wrong one.

Two related quirks in the same line, since they surprise people:

- `| 0` is a 32-bit signed conversion, and 36⁶ = 2,176,782,336 exceeds 2³¹−1. About 1.3% of the time the value wraps negative and `.toString(36)` emits a leading `-`, giving a double-dash slug like `my-title--1x2y3`. Ugly, not a collision.
- The suffix is not fixed-width — a small random value yields a short suffix (e.g. `-3k`). Rare, but slugs are not all the same shape.

Separately: `update()` never re-slugs, so renaming an article keeps the old slug — `src/article/article.service.ts:190-195` does `Object.assign(toUpdate, articleData)` and saves, with no `slugify` call.

Not read: the `slug` npm package's own normalization rules (so I can't say how it handles two titles differing only by punctuation/unicode — those *could* normalize to the same base, which the random suffix still separates), and any tests.
